title: Hangover Symptoms: A Head-to-Toe Guide and When to Worry
excerpt: Every common hangover symptom explained, from headache and nausea to anxiety and a racing heart: what causes each one, how long it lasts, and the warning signs that mean it is not just a hangover.
metaDescription: Hangover symptoms from head to toe: what causes each one, how long they last, and the signs that point to alcohol poisoning or withdrawal instead.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a hangover is the cluster of physical and mental symptoms that shows up after a night of drinking, usually starting as your blood alcohol level falls back toward zero. The most common symptoms are tiredness, thirst, headache, nausea, poor sleep, trouble concentrating, and a low or anxious mood. For most people they peak in the morning and fade within about 24 hours. A few symptoms are not part of a normal hangover at all, and those are the ones worth knowing: confusion you can't shake, repeated vomiting, a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, chest pain, seizures, or shaking and sweating that come back every time you stop drinking.

This guide walks through hangover symptoms from head to toe, explains what's causing each one in plain words, shows how long they usually last, and lays out the signs that mean something other than a hangover is going on.

> **When to see a doctor or get help now.** A normal hangover is miserable but harmless, and it improves through the day. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone** can't be woken, is confused or very slow to respond, is vomiting while drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing (fewer than 8 breaths a minute, or gaps of 10 seconds or more), has blue or very pale skin or lips, feels cold to the touch, or has a seizure. Those are signs of **alcohol poisoning**, which can still be developing the morning after a very heavy night. **See a doctor the same day if** you have chest pain, a heartbeat that stays fast or irregular, vomiting you can't keep water down through, blood in vomit or stool, a severe "worst ever" headache, yellow skin or eyes, or symptoms that are getting worse rather than better after 24 hours. **Talk to a doctor soon if** you get shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or anxiety that shows up when you *stop* drinking and eases when you drink again. That pattern is alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover, and it can become dangerous, so get medical advice before cutting down suddenly on your own. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## What Counts as a Hangover?

Researchers have spent years arguing about this, and in 2020 the Alcohol Hangover Research Group published a consensus definition. In plain words, a hangover is the combination of negative mental and physical symptoms that can follow a single episode of drinking, starting when blood alcohol concentration gets close to zero.

Two parts of that definition are useful for anyone trying to figure out what they're feeling:

- **It starts as the alcohol leaves.** A hangover is not the same as still being drunk. If you wake up after a very late, very heavy night, you may still have alcohol in your blood, which is why some people feel "fine" at 7am and terrible by 11am. The worst of it tends to arrive as your blood alcohol hits zero.
- **It follows a single episode.** Hangovers are about one night. Symptoms that show up every time you stop drinking after days or weeks of heavy use are a different thing (withdrawal), covered later in this guide.

## The Full List of Hangover Symptoms

Survey studies of drinkers, including work by Penning, McKinney, and Verster published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism* in 2012, found that fatigue and thirst were the symptoms people reported most often, followed by things like drowsiness, headache, dry mouth, nausea, weakness, and reduced alertness. Here is the broader list, grouped by where you feel it.

| Area | Common symptoms |
|---|---|
| Whole body | Fatigue, weakness, sleepiness, thirst, feeling cold or sweaty, general "poisoned" feeling |
| Head and brain | Headache, dizziness, poor concentration, slow thinking, memory fog, sensitivity to light and sound |
| Mood | Anxiety ("hangxiety"), low mood, irritability, guilt or regret, restlessness |
| Stomach and gut | Nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, heartburn, loss of appetite, diarrhea |
| Heart and circulation | Faster heartbeat, palpitations, flushed or pale skin |
| Muscles and joints | Body aches, stiffness, shaky hands |
| Sleep | Waking early, broken sleep, vivid dreams, feeling unrested |
| Mouth and eyes | Dry mouth, bad breath, red or puffy eyes, puffy face |

Not everyone gets every symptom, and the mix varies a lot from person to person and from night to night. Some people mostly get a headache; others mostly feel sick or anxious. That variation is one reason no single remedy works for everyone.

## Why Hangovers Happen: The Main Causes in Plain Words

A hangover isn't one problem. It's several things going wrong at once, and different symptoms trace back to different causes. A widely cited review by Swift and Davidson (1998) and later reviews by Penning and colleagues describe roughly the same set of contributors.

1. **Fluid loss.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water. You urinate more than you drink, which feeds thirst, dry mouth, dizziness, and headache. Dehydration is real, but researchers generally see it as one contributor rather than the whole story, because hangover severity doesn't track neatly with how dehydrated people are.
2. **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver breaks alcohol down first into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, and then into harmless acetate. If acetaldehyde builds up faster than you clear it, it can contribute to nausea, flushing, a fast heartbeat, and the general poisoned feeling. People whose enzymes clear it slowly (common in people of East Asian descent) tend to feel this strongly.
3. **Inflammation.** Studies have found raised levels of immune signaling molecules (cytokines) during hangovers. That's part of why a hangover can feel like the early stage of a cold or flu: aches, fatigue, low mood, and a foggy head.
4. **Poor sleep.** Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it breaks up sleep in the second half of the night and cuts into REM sleep. You wake earlier and less rested, which makes every other symptom feel worse.
5. **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol increases stomach acid and irritates the stomach lining, which adds to nausea, pain, and heartburn.
6. **Blood sugar dips.** Your liver puts alcohol first and makes less glucose while it's working on it. In some people, especially after drinking without food, this adds to shakiness, weakness, and irritability.
7. **Congeners.** These are by-products of fermentation and aging found in larger amounts in darker drinks like bourbon, brandy, and red wine. A controlled study by Rohsenow and colleagues (2010) found that bourbon produced somewhat worse hangovers than the same amount of vodka, although the amount of alcohol mattered far more than the type.
8. **The rebound effect.** Alcohol calms the brain while you're drinking. When it wears off, the brain briefly swings the other way, which is part of why some people feel jittery, sensitive to noise, and anxious the next day.

## Hangover Symptoms From Head to Toe

### Headache

The hangover headache is usually a dull, throbbing pain on both sides of the head, often worse when you move, bend over, or step into bright light. Fluid loss, changes in blood vessel tone, inflammation, and poor sleep all likely play a part. Water, food, and rest help; if you use a painkiller, use one carefully (more on that below). Our guide to [hangover headache relief](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) covers the options in more detail.

A headache that is sudden and severe, the worst you've ever had, or comes with a stiff neck, weakness on one side, slurred speech, or vision changes is not a hangover headache. Get emergency care.

### Brain fog, poor concentration, and dizziness

Slow thinking, poor memory, and difficulty focusing are some of the most consistent hangover effects in research. Studies have shown that reaction time and attention can stay impaired the morning after even when blood alcohol has returned to zero. That has a practical side: you may feel sober but still drive or work less safely than normal.

Dizziness usually comes from fluid loss and low blood pressure when you stand up quickly. Sit for a minute before getting up, and drink water. A spinning sensation that lasts all day, or dizziness with fainting, deserves a doctor's look.

More on this: [brain fog after drinking](/never-hungover/brain-fog-after-drinking).

### Anxiety and low mood

Many people wake up with a racing mind, a sense of dread, or embarrassment about the night before, often called "hangxiety." The rebound effect in the brain, poor sleep, low blood sugar, and fragments of memory all feed it. It's real and common, and it usually lifts as the rest of the hangover does. If you find it's a regular part of your mornings after drinking, our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) goes deeper into causes and what helps.

### Fatigue and sleepiness

Fatigue is the single most reported hangover symptom. Broken sleep is a big part of it, along with inflammation and the general work your body has been doing overnight. Alcohol's effect on the second half of the night is covered in our [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) explainer.

If the problem was the night itself, see [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking).

### Nausea, vomiting, and stomach pain

Nausea comes from a mix of stomach irritation, acetaldehyde, and slowed stomach emptying. Small sips of water or an oral rehydration drink, bland food once you can manage it, and ginger are the usual approaches. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers what tends to settle a stomach.

Vomiting once or twice the next morning is common. Vomiting that won't stop, prevents you from keeping water down for several hours, or contains blood (bright red or looking like coffee grounds) needs medical attention. So does severe stomach pain that spreads to your back, which can be a sign of pancreatitis.

More on this: [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking).

### Diarrhea and heartburn

Alcohol speeds up the gut and interferes with how the intestines absorb water, so loose stools the next day are common. It also relaxes the valve at the top of the stomach, which lets acid creep up and cause heartburn. Both usually settle within a day. Diarrhea that lasts more than a couple of days, or comes with fever or blood, is a reason to see a doctor.

More on these: [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) and [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking).

### Racing heart and palpitations

A heart rate that's higher than normal the morning after is common. Fluid loss, acetaldehyde, the rebound effect, and stress hormones all push it up. Occasionally, heavy drinking can trigger an irregular rhythm, most often atrial fibrillation, sometimes called "holiday heart." A heartbeat that is irregular (not just fast), comes with chest pain, shortness of breath, or fainting, or stays racing even while you're resting and hydrated, needs to be checked the same day.

More on this, including when it needs a doctor: [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking).

### Shaky hands, sweating, and feeling cold

Mild shakiness the morning after a big night can come from low blood sugar, poor sleep, and the nervous-system rebound. It should fade once you've eaten and rested. Sweating and feeling cold at the same time are also common, because alcohol widens blood vessels near the skin and disturbs temperature control.

The important distinction: shaking that appears whenever you go a day without alcohol, gets worse over hours, and eases when you drink is a sign of withdrawal, not a hangover. That needs medical advice (see below).

More on these: [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) and [night sweats after drinking](/never-hungover/night-sweats-after-drinking).

### Body aches and muscle soreness

Achy muscles and joints are often part of the inflammation story, along with a night of dancing, standing, or sleeping in an awkward position. Rest, fluids, and food help. Severe muscle pain with very dark, cola-colored urine is rare but serious and needs urgent care.

More on this: [body aches after drinking](/never-hungover/body-aches-after-drinking).

### Thirst and dry mouth

These come straight from fluid loss and from breathing through your mouth while sleeping. Water works, and an electrolyte drink can help if you've been vomiting or had diarrhea. Our comparison of [Pedialyte and Gatorade for hangovers](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) looks at what's in each.

### Puffy face, red eyes, and sensitivity to light and sound

Alcohol can cause fluid to shift and pool in the face and around the eyes, especially if you slept face down after salty food. Red eyes come from widened blood vessels and poor sleep. Many people also find bright light and loud noise harder to tolerate, likely part of the same nervous-system rebound that drives hangover anxiety.

## How Long Do Hangover Symptoms Last?

For most people, hangover symptoms peak in the morning, around the time blood alcohol returns to zero, and ease over the course of the day. Most are gone within about 24 hours. A very heavy night can push symptoms into a second day, and sleep problems and low mood can trail behind the physical symptoms.

| Symptom | Typical course |
|---|---|
| Thirst, dry mouth | Improves within hours of drinking fluids |
| Nausea, stomach upset | Usually eases by midday or afternoon |
| Headache | Often hours; can last most of the day |
| Fatigue, brain fog | Can linger into the evening |
| Low mood, anxiety | Often fades by the next day; can outlast physical symptoms |
| Disturbed sleep | Usually back to normal within a night or two |

Several things make hangovers longer or worse: drinking more, drinking faster, drinking on an empty stomach, poor sleep, being older, and drinking darker spirits. Our guides on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last), [two-day hangovers](/never-hungover/two-day-hangover), and [why hangovers get worse with age](/never-hungover/why-hangovers-get-worse-with-age) cover the timeline in more depth.

If you're no better after 24 hours, or you're getting worse instead of better, stop assuming it's a hangover. Something else may be going on.

## Hangover vs. Alcohol Poisoning: How to Tell the Difference

This is the most important comparison on this page. A hangover is unpleasant but not dangerous. Alcohol poisoning means there's enough alcohol in the body to suppress breathing, gag reflex, heart rate, and temperature control, and it can kill.

| Hangover | Alcohol poisoning |
|---|---|
| Starts as alcohol leaves the body | Happens while alcohol levels are high or still rising |
| You're awake and making sense, just feel awful | Confusion, stupor, or can't be woken |
| Vomiting is occasional and you can sit up | Vomiting while drowsy or passed out (choking risk) |
| Normal breathing | Slow or irregular breathing |
| Normal or slightly pale skin | Blue-tinged or very pale skin, cold to the touch |
| Gets better through the day | Can get worse even after drinking stops |

The reason the overlap matters: alcohol keeps being absorbed from the stomach and gut after the last drink. Someone who went to bed very drunk can still be at risk in the early morning hours. Never leave a person who's passed out from drinking to "sleep it off" alone, especially on their back.

**If you see any alcohol-poisoning sign, call 911.** While you wait, keep the person on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, keep them warm, and stay with them. Coffee, cold showers, and walking it off don't lower blood alcohol and can make things worse.

## Hangover vs. Alcohol Withdrawal

This section is short, but it matters.

A hangover follows one night of drinking and improves through the next day. Withdrawal happens when someone who has been drinking heavily on a regular basis stops or cuts back sharply. The brain has adjusted to alcohol being there, and when it's removed, the nervous system becomes overactive.

Signs that point toward withdrawal rather than a hangover:

- Shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or anxiety that **comes back every time** you go without a drink
- Symptoms that **get worse** over the first day or two without alcohol instead of better
- Symptoms that **ease when you drink**
- Trouble sleeping for several nights, seeing or hearing things that aren't there, or confusion
- Any seizure

Withdrawal can become dangerous, and in severe cases life-threatening. If this pattern sounds familiar, talk to a doctor before stopping on your own. They can make stopping safe. If someone has a seizure, severe confusion, or hallucinations, call 911.

## Hangover vs. Getting Sick

A hangover can feel a lot like a cold, the flu, or a stomach bug: tired, achy, nauseated, foggy. A few clues help separate them:

- **Fever.** A hangover doesn't usually cause a true fever (a measured temperature of 100.4°F / 38°C or higher). If you have one, it's more likely an infection.
- **Timeline.** Hangover symptoms ease through the day. An illness typically builds or sticks around for several days.
- **Sore throat, cough, or runny nose.** These aren't hangover symptoms.
- **Other people.** If the people you were with feel fine on the same amount, and you don't, consider that you might be coming down with something.

If you're unsure and feel unwell for more than a day, treat it as an illness and see a doctor if needed.

## Hangover Symptoms Without Drinking Much

Some people get noticeable hangover symptoms after only one or two drinks. Common reasons include drinking without food, poor sleep, smaller body size, age, certain medications, a slow-acting version of the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde, sensitivity to histamines or sulfites in wine, and simply not drinking often. Our guide on [why some people get hangovers so easily](/never-hungover/why-do-i-get-hangovers-so-easily) covers each of these.

If even small amounts of alcohol cause hives, wheezing, a swollen face or lips, or trouble breathing, that's an allergic-type reaction, not a hangover. Get emergency care for breathing trouble and see a doctor about it afterward.

## What Actually Helps With Hangover Symptoms

There is no good evidence that any product cures a hangover. A systematic review by Pittler and colleagues in the *BMJ* (2005) found no compelling evidence for any conventional or complementary hangover remedy, and the research since then is still thin. Time is the only thing that reliably ends a hangover. What you can do is ease specific symptoms while your body catches up.

- **Fluids.** Water for thirst, dry mouth, and dizziness. An oral rehydration drink if you've been vomiting or had diarrhea.
- **Food.** Something bland with carbohydrates and a little salt, like toast, crackers, rice, or soup, once your stomach allows it. This helps blood sugar and shakiness.
- **Sleep.** Even a nap helps with fatigue and brain fog.
- **Painkillers, carefully.** Ibuprofen or aspirin can help a headache but irritate a stomach that alcohol has already irritated, so take them with food. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is easier on the stomach but adds work for the liver; never take it before or while drinking, and don't stack it with other products that contain it. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the liver risk.
- **Caffeine in moderation.** A normal cup of coffee can help if you're used to it, but too much can worsen anxiety, a racing heart, and an upset stomach.
- **Skip the "hair of the dog."** Another drink only postpones the hangover, and it adds more alcohol for your liver to deal with.

Things that don't help: cold showers, sweating it out in a sauna (you'll lose more fluid), or heavy greasy food on a very queasy stomach.

## Preventing the Symptoms Next Time

The most effective prevention is the least exciting: drink less, drink more slowly, eat before and while you drink, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, and go to bed early enough to get real sleep. Clear spirits tend to cause somewhat milder hangovers than dark ones at the same dose, but the amount matters far more than the type. Our [hangover prevention guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes step by step through the habits with the best evidence, and the [hangover science hub](/never-hungover/complete-hangover-science-hub-2025) links every symptom and remedy guide on the site.

Some people also add a supplement. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the brain. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than settled. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in everyone, and it does nothing to protect you from alcohol poisoning or make it safe to drink more. If you want to try it as one part of a sensible drinking routine, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and if you take prescription medication, check with your pharmacist first.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What are the most common hangover symptoms?**

Fatigue and thirst are the most commonly reported, followed by headache, dry mouth, drowsiness, nausea, weakness, poor concentration, and low or anxious mood. Many people also get poor sleep, stomach upset, a faster heartbeat, and sensitivity to light and sound. The mix varies from person to person and night to night.

**How long do hangover symptoms last?**

Most hangovers peak in the morning, as blood alcohol returns to zero, and fade within about 24 hours. A very heavy night can stretch symptoms into a second day, and tiredness and low mood can linger after the physical symptoms ease. If you're getting worse rather than better after a day, see a doctor.

**When should I worry about hangover symptoms?**

Get emergency help for confusion, trouble waking, slow or irregular breathing, seizures, blue or very pale skin, or vomiting while drowsy. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning. See a doctor the same day for chest pain, an irregular or persistently racing heartbeat, vomiting that stops you keeping water down, blood in vomit or stool, yellow skin or eyes, or a sudden severe headache.

**How can I tell a hangover from alcohol poisoning?**

A hangover starts as the alcohol leaves your body; you feel awful but you're awake, making sense, and slowly improving. Alcohol poisoning happens while alcohol levels are high and involves confusion, stupor, slow or irregular breathing, vomiting while barely conscious, or cold, bluish skin. If you see any of those, call 911 and keep the person on their side.

**Is it a hangover or alcohol withdrawal?**

A hangover follows a single night of drinking and gets better through the next day. Withdrawal follows regular heavy drinking: shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or anxiety that come back whenever you go without a drink and ease when you drink. Withdrawal can become dangerous, so talk to a doctor before stopping suddenly if that pattern sounds familiar.

**Can a hangover cause a fever?**

A hangover can make you feel hot, cold, and sweaty, but it doesn't usually cause a true fever (100.4°F / 38°C or higher on a thermometer). A real fever, especially with a sore throat, cough, or symptoms lasting several days, points to an infection rather than a hangover.

**Why do I get hangover symptoms after only one or two drinks?**

Common reasons include drinking on an empty stomach, poor sleep, smaller body size, age, certain medications, genetic differences in how quickly you clear acetaldehyde, and sensitivity to compounds in some drinks such as wine. Hives, wheezing, or facial swelling after alcohol are an allergic-type reaction rather than a hangover and need medical attention.

**Is there anything that cures hangover symptoms?**

There is no good evidence that any product cures a hangover. Time is the only reliable fix. Water, a bland meal, sleep, and careful use of a painkiller can ease specific symptoms. Supplements such as DHM have some early research behind them, mostly in animals, but they are not a cure and don't make it safe to drink more.
